findings.description:
`_feedback_slice.py::parse_admissibility_block` accepts invalid or context-invalid admissibility statuses as passing evidence.

Premises:
1. The parser’s status regex is `r"(PASS|FAIL|N/A|NA)"` for `σ_measured` and `r"(PASS|FAIL)"` for other gates.
2. The regex has no right-hand token boundary.
3. Therefore `PASSIVE` matches `PASS`, and any word beginning with `PASS` is accepted as a valid pass status.
4. The parser also treats `σ_measured: N/A` as pass unconditionally.
5. FFAFP §15 permits `σ_measured: N/A` only when no fix measurement is applicable. If a finding includes a machine-parseable `FIX` block, `σ_measured: N/A` is not valid because post-fix verification is required.

Concrete examples:

Example A — malformed status accepted:
ADMISSIBILITY:
  S_min: PASSIVE
  G-completeness: PASS
  d_tool: PASS
  σ_measured: PASS
  q_retest: PASS
Current behavior:
- For `S_min`, regex `S_min\s*[:\-=]?\s*(PASS|FAIL)` matches the `PASS` prefix of `PASSIVE`.
- `found_pass=True`.
- `S_min` is not returned as failed.

Expected behavior:
- `PASSIVE` is not one of `{PASS, FAIL}`.
- `S_min` should be returned as failed.

Example B — fix present but `σ_measured: N/A` accepted:
FIX:
<<<< SEARCH bench/foo.py
old
====
new
>>>> REPLACE

ADMISSIBILITY:
  S_min: PASS
  G-completeness: PASS
  d_tool: PASS
  σ_measured: N/A
  q_retest: PASS
Current behavior:
- `σ_measured` status `N/A` is treated as pass.
- The parser returns no failure for `σ_measured`.

Expected behavior:
- A machine-parseable fix exists.
- `σ_measured` must be measured post-fix, so `N/A` should fail.

The `section_terminator` regex in `parse_admissibility_block` (line ~109) uses `re.MULTILINE` with `^` anchors, but the `tail` string is a substring of the original `finding_text` starting at an arbitrary offset. The `^` anchor matches the start of the *string*, not the start of a line, when the string does not begin at a line boundary. If the `ADMISSIBILITY:` marker is not at the start of a line (e.g., it appears mid-line after some prefix text), `marker_match` will still find it (since the marker regex uses `^` with `re.MULTILINE` on the full `finding_text`), but `tail` will begin mid-line. The subsequent `section_terminator` regex also uses `^` with `re.MULTILINE` on `tail`. If `tail` starts mid-line, the first line of `tail` will not match `^` because `^` only matches after newlines in `re.MULTILINE` mode, not at the start of a string that begins mid-line. This means a section header on the same line as the `ADMISSIBILITY:` marker (or immediately after it without a newline) will not be detected as a terminator, causing the block to consume more text than intended.

findings.description:
The `gate_patterns` list for `G-completeness` includes the pattern `r"G completeness"` (with a space), but the `status_pattern` regex that follows requires `[:\-=]?\s*` between the gate name and the status. The pattern `r"G completeness"` followed by `r"\s*[:\-=]?\s*"` would match `G completeness: PASS` (space, then optional separator, then PASS). However, if a model writes `G completeness PASS` (space, no colon), the regex `G completeness\s*[:\-=]?\s*PASS` would match because `\s*` matches the space and `[:\-=]?` is optional. This is actually fine — the permissive matching works.

But there's a subtler issue: the `gate_patterns` for `G-completeness` includes `r"G[-_\s]+completeness"`. This pattern uses `+` (one or more), which means it requires at least one separator character between "G" and "completeness". The canonical form is "G-completeness" (with a hyphen). If a model writes "Gcompleteness" (no separator), it won't match. But this is arguably correct — "Gcompleteness" is not a valid gate name.

The actual edge case: the pattern `r"G[-_\s]+completeness"` would match "G completeness" (with a space), but the separate pattern `r"G completeness"` is redundant since `[-_\s]+` already covers spaces. This is not a bug, just redundant code.

More concerning: the `gate_patterns` list is extended with `extend`, which adds patterns to the list. But the loop `for pat in gate_patterns:` iterates over all patterns including the original `re.escape(gate)`. For `G-completeness`, `re.escape("G-completeness")` produces `"G\\-completeness"`, which matches the literal string "G-completeness". The extended patterns add alternative spellings. This is correct.

I cannot find a genuine bug here beyond the heading-marker issue in F001. Let me look deeper.

Actual Bug: The `section_terminator` regex uses `re.MULTILINE` but the `tail` string may not start at a line boundary, causing `^` to fail for the first line.

Wait, I already analysed this above and concluded it works because `re.MULTILINE` makes `^` match at string start AND after newlines. Even if `tail` starts mid-line, `^` matches at position 0 of `tail`. The issue would only arise if a section header appeared on the same line as the ADMISSIBILITY marker without a newline, e.g.:
ADMISSIBILITY: S_min: PASS NOVELTY: ...
Here `tail` = ` S_min: PASS NOVELTY: ...`. The `section_terminator` regex `^\s*NOVELTY\s*:` would need to match `NOVELTY:` but it's on the same line as other content. `^\s*` matches at position 0 (start of `tail`), then `\s*` matches the leading space, then it looks for `NOVELTY` but finds `S_min`. No match. The regex engine continues searching and finds `NOVELTY:` later in the string, but `^` won't match mid-line even with `re.MULTILINE` because there's no newline before `NOVELTY`. So the terminator fails to match, and the block consumes everything. This is a parser-runaway scenario.

However, this requires the ADMISSIBILITY content and the next section to be on the same line, which is unlikely in practice (models typically put each section on its own line). Severity is low.
findings.proposed_fix: No fix proposed — the scenario is too unlikely to justify complicating the parser. Document as a known limitation.

findings.description: The `parse_admissibility_block` function returns `List[str]` but the type annotation uses `from typing import List` (capital-L), which is deprecated in Python 3.9+ in favour of `list[str]` (lowercase-l builtin). The code includes `from __future__ import annotations` which enables PEP 585 behaviour, making `List[str]` valid at runtime, but the import of `List` from `typing` is unnecessary and triggers deprecation warnings in Python 3.9+. This is a MEDIUM finding per the proof-of-concept context — it doesn't affect correctness but indicates stale typing practices.

findings.description:
`parse_admissibility_block` only terminates the ADMISSIBILITY block at a hard-coded list of section headers, so a valid later all-caps section not in that list can be swallowed into the ADMISSIBILITY block and mask missing gates.

Location: `bench/logs/exp40_slice_admissibility_hardened_20260518T190104Z/working/_feedback_slice.py`, inside `parse_admissibility_block`, at the `section_terminator = re.search(...)` block.

Evidence with concrete input:
ADMISSIBILITY:
  S_min: PASS (location supplied)
DIVERGENCE:
  G-completeness: PASS (alternative discussion text)
  d_tool: PASS (alternative discussion text)
  σ_measured: PASS (alternative discussion text)
  q_retest: PASS (alternative discussion text)

`parse_admissibility_block` returns false total failure (all 5 gates) when the ADMISSIBILITY block uses an inline format — i.e., gate content starts on the same line as the marker. The marker regex at line 58–62 uses a `$` anchor after the optional parenthetical:
r"^\s*(?:#{1,6}\s*)?ADMISSIBILITY\s*:?\s*(?:\([^)]*\))?\s*$"
Input like `ADMISSIBILITY: S_min: PASS | G-completeness: PASS | ...` (all on one line) fails the `$` match because `S_min: PASS ...` follows the colon on the same line. The function falls through to `return list(ADMISSIBILITY_GATES)` — silently reporting all five gates as FAIL when the model actually reported them all as PASS.

Confirmed via tool execution: `'ADMISSIBILITY: S_min: PASS'` → NO MATCH; `'ADMISSIBILITY:\n  S_min: PASS'` → MATCH.

findings.description:
The `σ_measured` gate has a coverage gap for the Unicode σ with whitespace separator. The parser provides two patterns for this gate: (1) `re.escape('σ_measured')` → matches literal `σ_measured` only, (2) `r"sigma[_\s]*measured"` → matches ASCII `sigma` with flexible separator. Neither matches `σ measured` (Unicode σ, space instead of underscore). Confirmed by tool execution:

- Pattern `'σ_measured'` on `'σ measured: PASS'` → NO MATCH
- Pattern `r'sigma[_\s]*measured'` on `'σ measured: PASS'` → NO MATCH
- Pattern `r'σ[_\s]*measured'` on `'σ measured: PASS'` → MATCH

The docstring claims the parser "accepts the σ character or the ASCII 'sigma' spelling" and is "whitespace-tolerant", but the Unicode σ variant is only matched with a literal underscore.

```text
  G-completeness: PASS
  d_tool: PASS
  σ_measured: PASS
  q_retest: PASS
```

- For `S_min`, regex `S_min\s*[:\-=]?\s*(PASS|FAIL)` matches the `PASS` prefix of `PASSIVE`.
- `found_pass=True`.
- `S_min` is not returned as failed.

Expected behavior:
- `PASSIVE` is not one of `{PASS, FAIL}`.

```text
  G-completeness: PASS
  d_tool: PASS
  σ_measured: N/A
  q_retest: PASS
```
Current behavior:
- `σ_measured` status `N/A` is treated as pass.
- The parser returns no failure for `σ_measured`.

Expected behavior:
- A machine-parseable fix exists.
- `σ_measured` must be measured post-fix, so `N/A` should fail.

FOLLOW: This parser feeds the §17 feedback channel by identifying missing or failed admissibility gates. If invalid statuses such as `PASSIVE` are treated as `PASS`, malformed findings avoid corrective feedback. If a finding proposes a parseable fix but reports `σ_measured: N/A`, the feedback channel fails to require post-fix verification. Downstream consequence: inadmissible fixes can be treated as admissibility-clean, which weakens the experiment’s hardening target and can silently contaminate convergence metrics with unverified fixes.

ANALYSE: HARD constraint.

Premises:
- FFAFP §15 requires explicit PASS/FAIL/N/A gate reporting, with `σ_measured: N/A` only applicable when no post-fix measurement exists.
- The code’s status parser is responsible for detecting failed or absent gate compliance.
- A regex alternation without a token boundary accepts prefixes.

Derivation:
- `re.search(r"S_min\s*[:\-=]?\s*(PASS|FAIL)", "S_min: PASSIVE", re.I)` matches `PASS` because the pattern does not require the status token to end.
- Therefore the parser classifies an invalid status token as a valid pass.
- For `σ_measured`, the code explicitly treats `N/A` and `NA` as pass without checking whether the finding contains a machine-parseable fix.
- Therefore the parser cannot enforce the required distinction between “no fix, measurement not applicable” and “fix proposed, measurement required.”

Scoped null-alternative justification:
- Considered alternative 1: make downstream validation handle this instead. Rejected because this function is the component producing failed gate names for feedback; allowing false passes here suppresses the feedback signal.
- Considered alternative 2: reject all `σ_measured: N/A`. Rejected because no-fix findings legitimately use `N/A`.
- Considered alternative 3: implement a full grammar. Rejected as unnecessary for this proof-of-concept slice; a token boundary plus machine-fix check is the simplest sufficient correction.

Conclusion: CONFIRMED.

If the `ADMISSIBILITY:` marker is not at the start of a line (e.g., it appears mid-line after some prefix text), `marker_match` will still find it (since the marker regex uses `^` with `re.MULTILINE` on the full `finding_text`), but `tail` will begin mid-line. The subsequent `section_terminator` regex also uses `^` with `re.MULTILINE` on `tail`. If `tail` starts mid-line, the first line of `tail` will not match `^` because `^` only matches after newlines in `re.MULTILINE` mode, not at the start of a string that begins mid-line. This means a section header on the same line as the `ADMISSIBILITY:` marker (or immediately after it without a newline) will not be detected as a terminator, causing the block to consume more text than intended.

Concrete example:
```
finding_text = "SOME_PREFIX ADMISSIBILITY:\n  S_min: PASS\nNOVELTY: ..."
```
Here `marker_match` finds `ADMISSIBILITY:` at position 12. `tail = finding_text[28:]` = `"\n  S_min: PASS\nNOVELTY: ..."`. The `section_terminator` regex with `^` and `re.MULTILINE` will match `NOVELTY:` on the third line because `tail` starts with `\n`, so the first character is a newline and `^` matches after it. This case works.

But consider:
```
finding_text = "ADMISSIBILITY: S_min: PASS\nNOVELTY: ..."
```
Here `marker_match` finds `ADMISSIBILITY:` at position 0. `tail = finding_text[14:]` = `" S_min: PASS\nNOVELTY: ..."`. The `section_terminator` regex with `^` and `re.MULTILINE` will NOT match `NOVELTY:` because `tail` starts with a space, not a newline, and `^` only matches at string start (which is mid-line) or after newlines. The first line of `tail` is `" S_min: PASS"` — `^` matches at position 0 of `tail`, but `NOVELTY:` is on the second line. Wait — `re.MULTILINE` makes `^` match at the start of the string AND after each newline. So `^NOVELTY` should match at position after `\n`. Let me re-examine.

Actually, `tail = " S_min: PASS\nNOVELTY: ..."`. The `^` with `re.MULTILINE` matches at position 0 (start of string) and position 14 (after `\n`). So `^NOVELTY` would match at position 14. This case works.

The real failure case is when the ADMISSIBILITY block content and the next section header are on the same line without a newline separator, or when `tail` starts with content that includes a section header name but not at line start. However, the more significant issue is:

If `finding_text` contains `ADMISSIBILITY:` at the very end of the string with no trailing newline, `tail` is empty string `""`. Then `section_terminator` returns `None`, `block = tail` (empty string), and all gates fail — which is correct behaviour (missing block = all gates fail).

If the input text has the ADMISSIBILITY block indented (e.g., inside a markdown code block or quoted text), both regexes will fail to match because `^` matches start of line, and indented text has leading whitespace that `^\s*` handles. Wait — `^\s*` DOES handle leading whitespace. So indentation is fine.

This works fine — `NOVELTY:` is on its own line after `\n`.

Here `FIND` appears in the evidence text but not at line start, so it's fine.
